summary: Describes basic and advanced multimedia conferencing scenarios involving voice, video and text. They help define and evaluate the protocols developed in the centralized conferencing XCON working group. It is an informational document.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a set of story examples of group calls, such as a class with a teacher, to help designers work out what tools they need.

subtitle: A catalogue of group call stories, from simple dial-in meetings to sidebars, coaching and moderated chat, used to shape conferencing protocols.

tldr.problem: The XCON working group needed concrete examples of how people use multimedia conferences before defining protocols for centralized conferencing.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes basic scenarios for conference-unaware participants, advanced scenarios for conference-aware user agents, a list of advanced features, and scenarios for media policy control such as video layouts, sidebars and text chat.
tldr.outcome: It is Informational. It is explicitly not a requirements list, but a set of examples to help define and evaluate the XCON protocols.

today: RFC 4597 is an Informational document from August 2006. According to the unit metadata it has not been obsoleted or updated. It gives scenarios, not a protocol or a requirements list.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 4597 describes multimedia conferencing scenarios to help define and evaluate requirements for the centralized conferencing (XCON) working group. It uses some conventions from the SIP Conferencing Framework (RFC 4353), but the scenarios are not specific to SIP.

The Conferencing System is the center point for signaling, and the participant who starts a conference is the initiating participant. The scenarios apply to audio-only as well as audio and video, and to media such as text, interactive text or presentation graphics. The advanced scenarios assume user agents that support the XCON protocols, but many features can be done today with an interactive voice response (IVR) system or a web interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Before building a tool for group calls, the designers wrote down many everyday stories about how people use them.

sections.title: Basic Conferencing Scenarios
sections.content:
Basic scenarios let a conference-unaware participant create, join and take part in a conference. Typical minimum needs are DTMF tones or voice replies to an IVR system.

  • Ad hoc: a participant with a provisioned service calls the Conferencing System and a conference is created automatically. They tell others how to call in by instant message or email. If the owner must be authenticated first, early callers hear an announcement and are placed on hold.
  • Extending a point-to-point call: PA is in a call with PB and wants to add PC. Neither supports call transfer, so PA passes conference details to PB, both hang up and call the Conferencing System, which may dial out to PC.
  • Reserved: booked in advance by out-of-band means. A routable conference identification, a URI or a phone number with a pin number, is sent to participants, and the system can dial out to them.
sections.plainLanguage: In the simple stories, you just phone a special number and the call bridge puts everyone together, like a group phone line.

sections.title: Advanced Scenarios and Features
sections.content:
Advanced scenarios assume user agents that support at least call transfer and a way to receive conference events. A call can be extended without consultation (PA moves the call to the Conferencing System, then adds the third party) or with consultation (PA holds the current party, calls the third party, then transfers everyone). In lecture mode a lecturer presents, knows who the participants are, and can give them the right to speak using floor control or an out-of-band mechanism. A conference can mix conference-aware and unaware participants, with a proxy such as an IVR or web page for the unaware. Privileges may be given to the initiating participant, who may delegate them.

Section 3.5 lists example features, explicitly not a requirement list. They include adding and deleting participants, switching user agent or media mid-conference, authenticating and authorizing participants, controlling whose media is sent where, giving privileges, sidebars, conference information, extending a time-limited conference, audio-only and passive participants, recorders, whisper or private messages, and calling a human operator.
sections.plainLanguage: Smarter phones can do more, such as passing a call along, muting people, whispering to one person, or recording the call, if they have permission.

sections.title: Media Policy Control Scenarios
sections.content:
Authorized participants control media with a media control protocol or a third-party application. Video examples let the participant pick a predefined layout: single view, dual view, 4 streams in a 2x2 grid, 9 in 3x3, 16 in 4x4, or a 5+1 view where one window takes 4/9 of the screen and five take 1/9 each.

Other scenarios include:

  • Voice-activated video switch: everyone hears the N loudest participants but not themselves, and sees the loudest speaker.
  • Sidebar: a side conversation that may or may not include the main conference audio. A participant can be in more than one sidebar but actively in only one.
  • Coaching: a hidden supervisor who is not on the roster listens in and is heard only by the supervised participant.
  • Presentation and Q and A: only panel streams are mixed, then the chair switches the conference to normal or uses floor control.
  • Presence-enabled ad hoc conference: a walkie-talkie style talk button checks presence first.
  • Text scenarios: group chat, interactive text over RTP as in RFC 4103, moderated chat, text sidebars and moderator announcements.
sections.plainLanguage: These stories show who gets to see and hear whom: the loudest speaker on screen, a private side chat, or a boss quietly listening in.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Conferences usually have authorization rules, called the conference policy, about who may join and what media may be used. To enforce them the Conferencing System must be able to authenticate potential participants, for example with challenge and response, certificates, a shared secret or an asserted identity.

Content often needs to be confidential, so the system needs functions for securing the media and for key management and distribution. Privacy also matters: users may want to listen in silently or hide their identity while others know they are present. These requirements are discussed further in the XCON framework document.
sections.plainLanguage: A group call needs a guest list, a lock on the door, and sometimes a way to listen quietly without being named.
